questions.q: What is the key difference between the elicitation checklist from Lesson 8 and the review checklist from this lesson?
options: The elicitation checklist asks whether requirements were identified during discovery; the review checklist asks whether a design that's already been built actually delivered what was identified
They are the same checklist, just run at different times for no real reason
The elicitation checklist only applies to compliance, while the review checklist only applies to performance
The review checklist is run by executives, while the elicitation checklist is run only by developers
questions.explain: Elicitation asks 'did we identify what's needed?' early in the project. Review asks 'did we actually build what was identified?' later — these can diverge over a project as deadlines compress and decisions get made under pressure.

questions.q: Why does this lesson insist that a security checklist item shouldn't pass just because the permission set configuration looks correct on review?
options: Because permission sets are deprecated in favor of profiles
Because field-level security cannot be configured through permission sets
Because Security Health Check always contradicts the permission set configuration
Because the actual access behavior should be verified by testing with a real user assigned the relevant profile, not just assumed correct from reading the configuration
questions.explain: Reading a configuration and assuming it behaves as intended is not the same as verifying it — the checklist calls for actually testing with a user in the relevant profile to confirm the real behavior matches the security NFR.

questions.q: What distinguishes an "evidence-based pass" from a verbal-assurance pass on this lesson's checklist?
options: An evidence-based pass requires executive sign-off only, with no technical detail

An evidence-based pass is supported by documented proof — a specific test result, date, and measured number — that can be defended later or handed to the next architect, rather than just an assurance that something was done
There is no real difference; both are equally valid ways to mark a checklist item
An evidence-based pass only applies to the compliance category
questions.explain: The lesson contrasts 'Performance: pass' based on a quick click-through feeling fast against a documented load test with a specific date, simulated volume, and measured percentile result — only the latter can be defended later or verified by someone else.

questions.q: What does this lesson call a checklist run mechanically, where no one is willing to mark an item as failed?
options: A compliance audit
A load test
Checklist theater — producing false confidence that something was verified when it actually wasn't
A trace pattern
questions.explain: Checklist theater is the term this lesson uses for a review run with no real willingness to fail an item — it creates the appearance of verification without the substance, which is worse than not running the checklist at all.

questions.q: What does the maintainability/recoverability line item of this checklist specifically ask about backups?
options: Whether a working, tested backup and restore process actually exists — distinguishing 'we have backups' as a real tested capability from a claim nobody has ever verified by attempting an actual restore
Whether a backup configuration screen exists in Setup
Whether backups are stored in a Big Object
Whether the backup schedule matches the performance NFR's target response time
questions.explain: The checklist specifically distinguishes a backup process that has actually been tested with a real restore attempt from 'we have backups' as an unverified claim — only the tested version counts as a real pass.
